sources.title: Dash Academy curriculum — module 2 manifest row

claims.text: Dash is organized into two layers: Core (layer 1) settles Dash payments and provides governance, while Platform (layer 2) stores and verifies structured application data via data contracts, documents, identities, and signed state transitions.

A Dash payment reaches confirmation in about a second, at no extra cost, because every transaction is InstantSend-locked and blocks are ChainLocked — practical for checkout and user-facing payment flows.

Dash has no general-purpose smart-contract VM today: developers declare data with JSON-Schema data contracts instead of deploying code, which removes whole classes of smart-contract vulnerabilities; a VM is planned for Platform v4.0.

Dash's clearest non-fit is arbitrary on-chain computation — anything that needs a Turing-complete VM or heavy custom code per node — while its clear fits are payments, verifiable app data with proofs, identities/usernames, tokens, and digital assets.

DPNS registers human-readable .dash names (e.g. alice.dash) and ties them to a Platform identity, giving name-based interaction; premium names go through a masternode vote, ordinary names register immediately.

NFTs on Dash are documents, not a separate token standard: each document has a unique ID analogous to an ERC-721 token ID, plus built-in transfer, set-price purchase, mutation, deletion, and creation-restriction options.

Fungible tokens are first-class protocol objects declared in a data contract (no smart contract): minting, max supply, freeze/pause, burning, scheduled and perpetual distribution, and groups with voting thresholds are configured declaratively and enforced by the protocol.

Credits are a distinct unit of account from Dash: they are created at exactly 1000 credits per duff (1 DASH = 100,000,000,000 credits) by locking Dash on Core via an asset lock, and are spent on layer-2 fees.

Platform fees are storage fees plus processing fees, scaled by a network-governed fee multiplier, with a refund when stored data is deleted and a user fee increase to prioritize inclusion during congestion.
Credits can be converted back to Dash through the identity credit withdrawal state transition, subject to a network-wide daily limit; anyone may top up any identity, so apps can subsidize user fees.

Layer-1 transaction privacy comes from CoinJoin (formerly PrivateSend), a non-custodial mixing service coordinated by masternodes, so a user shuffles their Dash with others without trusting a third party.

Platform defines a shielded pool using Orchard/Halo2 zero-knowledge proofs for credits and tokens, with shield/unshield/shielded-transfer state transitions; however the shielded DAPI endpoints are defined in the protocol but not yet available on public nodes.

Dash is the world's first and longest-running DAO: a treasury funded by a portion of the block subsidy pays approved proposals, and masternodes — which hold 1000 DASH as collateral — vote on how treasury funds are spent.
Platform clients verify query responses with cryptographic proofs rather than trusting the node that served them, giving a light client full-node-equivalent security guarantees.

uncertainties.topic: How to frame the Platform shielded pool given its DAPI endpoints are not yet public
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson names the effect and defers the machinery: CoinJoin is live on layer 1 for Dash, and Platform adds a zero-knowledge shielded pool that is protocol-defined and rolling out, without asserting it is usable on public nodes today.

uncertainties.topic: Whether to cite the exact credits-per-duff ratio for Dash versus Credits
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson states the distinction (Dash is money, credits are the fee unit) and cites the exact conversion 1,000 credits per duff / 1 DASH = 100,000,000,000 credits, since the ratio is citable from protocol constants and is the kind of concrete fact the quiz can test.

uncertainties.topic: How deep to go on token/NFT/identity content without duplicating later modules
uncertainties.resolution: The lesson keeps to effects — configurable tokens, document-based NFTs, .dash usernames — in one or two sentences each and defers configuration and action mechanics to modules 15 and 16.
